newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's embattled Kia group turns to government.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's embattled Kia group turns to government.

text.p: South Korea's Kia Group, besieged by rumours of financial troubles that have left lenders increasingly skittish, has asked for the government's help to keep its credit lines open, Kia officials said on Tuesday.

"No company in the country would survive if lenders stopped providing credit in the way they are doing to us now," said Oh Min-boo, senior managing director of the beleaguered group's planning and co-ordinating office.
He warned that a growing reluctance by financial institutions to extend credits was damaging the nation's industrial competitiveness.
Oh said group chairman Kim Sun-hong had asked finance minister Kang Kyong-shik to persuade merchant banks to keep cash flowing to the eighth-ranked conglomerate.
"Malicious rumours about us have created unnecessary problems. We can see our overseas partners are now concerned," Oh said.
Some 5,000 Kia sub-contractors and 4,000 overseas sales outlets have expressed their concerns, a Kia statement said.

The group has been rumoured to be in financial trouble for months, but speculation grew in early June when a report leaked by Samsung Motors alleged "managerial conflicts" at group flagship Kia Motors and hinted at a takeover.
Shares of Kia affiliates, including group Kia Motors and Asia Motors, have taken a beating in recent days.
Analysts said South Korea's financial community turned nervous after the collapse of Hanbo Steel in January and Sammi Steel Co in March.
Kia's difficulties were exacerbated because the Samsung report, which was widely publicised, also suggested the nation's crowded car industry needed to be restructured to survive.

Kia Motors has been viewed as an easy takeover target because of the company's thinly spread shareholdings. Kia's largest shareholder Ford Motor Co holds 16.91 percent, with no management rights. Kia employees hold 13.81 percent.

"The takeover rumours are a major cause for Kia's problems," said Kim Byoung-joon, an analyst at Dongwon Economic Research Institute. "Kia has some problems as other companies do. But the group's trouble is definitely overblown."
Kang Hoon-suk, an analyst at ING Baring Securities, said: "Kia is simply facing an unfortunate situation. I don't see Kia's problems as serious."
Company officials said Kia affiliates would restructure.
Asia Motors, the group's commercial vehicle arm, would raise about 520 billion won by moving its plant to a cheaper site two to three years ahead of schedule.
The group also said it would sell some 795 billion won worth of idle assets.
Analysts praised the self-rescue plans.
Kia Motors' financial status was already well in line with the average of the nation's major conglomerates, they said.
Kia Motors' total debts were estimated at 5.6 trillion won at the end of 1996, against net worth of 1.3 trillion won and its entire assets of 2.68 trillion won.
The company's car exports have expanded 40 percent this year from a year ago, according to Kia officials.
"I don't understand why some financial institutions have shied away from giving us credits," Kia's Oh said.
Later on Tuesday, the finance ministry reaffirmed a plan first announced in May to probe unfair loan calls by merchant banks.
"If merchant banks unfairly call in loans from companies with sound financial conditions for no reason, the ministry will launch an investigation," a ministry official said.
"We can say the Kia Group is a sound enterprise," the official said.
